Triggers.value: Specific body parts associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
Being alone in a room or building
hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings

Threat.value: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

vignette:
Ethan is a 21-year-old man who presents with a quiet, almost haunted stillness. He speaks in short, halting sentences, his gaze often fixed on a point just past the therapist's shoulder. He has not worked in four months, having lost his job at a local distribution centre, and now rarely leaves the small apartment he shares with his wife, Chloe. The event that changed everything, he explains, happened six months ago. They were walking home from a late movie, taking a familiar shortcut through a poorly lit side street, when a man stepped out from a recessed doorway. The memory doesn't exist for Ethan as a coherent narrative he can recount; he says he can’t seem to put the frightening event into words. Instead, it lives in him as a series of stark, photographic stills: Chloe’s arm twisted behind her back, the man’s thick, veiny hands, the terrified look in her eyes. Sometimes, when these images flash through his mind, he can smell the cheap, cloying cologne the attacker wore.

In the months since, Ethan has come to believe he is fundamentally broken. The memory of his own paralysis during the assault serves as constant, irrefutable evidence that he cannot rely on himself in a crisis (**Memory → Negative Appraisals**). This deep-seated conviction that he is no longer capable of protecting anyone, least of all himself, has made the world feel intensely dangerous. It has primed him to see threats everywhere; he now scans faces in a crowd, his attention snagging on anyone who seems out of place or moves too quickly (**Negative Appraisals → Triggers**). A simple comment from a relative asking how Chloe is doing can feel like an accusation, a trigger that sends a hot spike of shame through him. When these triggers arise—a suspicious-looking person on the street, a news report about a local crime—the photographic fragments of the assault invade his mind, sharp and vivid as the moment they happened (**Triggers → Memory**).

This constant sense of being under siege has reshaped his life into a series of defensive manoeuvres. The feeling of immediate threat, of his body tensing for a fight he feels he has already lost, is overwhelming (**Triggers → Threat**). This feeling has become so entwined with his environment that he is always on guard, startling violently at sudden movements by others (**Threat → Triggers**). To manage this unbearable state of arousal, he has systematically eliminated anything that might provoke it. He avoids watching any television shows or films that involve violence, changing the channel frantically if a crime drama appears (**Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies**). The intrusive images themselves are so agonizing that he will do anything to stop them; he can no longer bear to be by himself, convinced that danger lurks just outside the door and that he would be powerless to stop it (**Memory → Maladaptive Strategies**). His fear is a constant companion, and in its presence, he clings to Chloe, a decision that only reinforces his belief that the world is unsafe and he is inadequate to face it alone (**Threat → Maladaptive Strategies**).

These strategies, meant to keep him safe, have instead built a prison. By refusing to be alone, he has inadvertently taught his nervous system that solitude itself is a threat, which only heightens his baseline anxiety (**Maladaptive Strategies → Threat**). This avoidance also prevents the fragmented, nonverbal memories from ever being processed, keeping them frozen and potent, ready to ambush him at the slightest provocation (**Maladaptive Strategies → Memory**). Paradoxically, the more he avoids, the more sensitive he becomes, and the list of triggers grows, shrinking his world further (**Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers**). His body feels like an enemy, betraying him with a racing heart and shallow breath even when he is sitting on his own couch (**Threat → Negative Appraisals**). He can’t sleep through the night, jerking awake from nightmares where he is reliving the attack, frozen and useless. When the pressure of the memories and the feeling of imminent danger become too much to bear, he has started hurting himself, digging his nails into his own arms until he bleeds, a desperate act to release the overwhelming feelings and replace the psychological pain with a physical one.

He finally sought therapy after Chloe found the marks on his arm. The shame was profound, but it was eclipsed by his terror of losing her. He feels he is no longer the man she married, just a collection of fears and failures. He sits in the therapy room, a young man trapped in a feedback loop of his own making, hoping for a way out but deeply afraid that he is permanently damaged, that the capable person he once was is gone for good.
